chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Hammad from Hariz from Zurarah and Muhammad ibn Muslim and Abu Basir and Burayd al-Ajli and al-Fudayl from Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon them):

In the sheep: for every forty sheep, one sheep is due, and there is nothing due for less than forty. Then there is nothing due until it reaches two hundred and ten; when it reaches two hundred and ten, one sheep is due. If it exceeds two hundred and ten, two sheep are due, and there is nothing more than two sheep until it reaches two hundred. When it reaches two hundred, the same applies. If it exceeds two hundred, one sheep is due, so three sheep are due. Then there is nothing more than that until it reaches three hundred. When it reaches three hundred, three sheep are due. If one is added, four sheep are due, until it reaches four hundred. When four hundred are complete, for every hundred one sheep is due, and the previous rule is dropped, and there is nothing due for less than a hundred after that, and there is nothing due for the 'niyyf' (the extra sheep beyond the hundred).
And they (Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah) said: "Whatever does not have the year pass over it while in possession, there is no khums/zakat due on it; when the year passes over it, it becomes due."

key_terms.النَّيِّف: The extra sheep beyond a round number (e.g., 101-109)
key_terms.الْحَوْل: The passing of a full year

ai.seo_question: What are the specific thresholds and rates for khums or zakat on sheep according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the detailed *nisab* (minimum threshold) and *qadar* (quantity) for *zakat al-ghanam* (zakat on sheep), reflecting the juristic consensus on the graduated scale of liability. It emphasizes the condition of *hawl* (lunar year) as the trigger for obligation, a principle central to Shia fiqh regarding livestock. The text serves as a primary source for calculating charitable dues in agricultural and pastoral contexts within Shia legal tradition.
